STEP 7: when the object is a person, the personal «a» disappears along with the name: «Veo a Ana» becomes «La veo». STEP 8: Spanish never lets you drop this pronoun once the object has already been mentioned: «¿Viste la película? — Sí, la vi».
topicos.comparacao: English object pronouns (it, him, her, them) are required too, just like Spanish, so the underlying habit of never dropping the object isn't new ground — English speakers already do this instinctively. What genuinely is new is word order: English object pronouns always sit after the verb («I bought it», «I saw her»), while Spanish puts the pronoun before the conjugated verb («Lo compré», «La vi») or attaches it directly onto an infinitive with no space and no hyphen («comprarlo») — a position English has no equivalent for at all.

exemplos.ru: Busco el paraguas, pero no lo encuentro.
exemplos.pt: I'm looking for the umbrella, but I can't find it.

exemplos.ru: Quiero comprarlas hoy.
exemplos.pt: I want to buy them today.

exemplos.ru: ¿Has visto a Marta? — Sí, la he visto esta mañana.
exemplos.pt: Did you see Marta? Yes, I saw her this morning.

erros.motivo: The direct object pronoun is required in Spanish.
Spanish never uses a subject-style word like «él» as the object; it uses «lo».
The pronoun attaches to the infinitive with no hyphen.
The pronoun comes before the conjugated verb.
In the negative, «no» comes before the pronoun, which sits before the verb.

topicos.titulo: Me, te, nos, os, usted, and the neuter «lo»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: when the direct object is the speaker or the listener, the pronouns are «me» (me), «te» (you, tú), «nos» (us), and «os» (you-all, vosotros). «Me llamas», «Te espero», «Nos invitan», «Os visito». STEP 2: «usted» and «ustedes» follow the third-person pattern: «Lo llamo mañana, señor Ruiz» and «La ayudo, señora». For ustedes: «Los llamo» or «Las llamo». STEP 3: «me», «te», «nos», and «os» also work as indirect objects; only the third person changes. Lesson 24 covers the indirect object. STEP 4: «lo» can also stand in for an idea rather than a noun. This is called the «neuter lo»: «No lo sé» (I don't know), «Ya lo sabía» (I already knew that), «Lo entiendo» (I understand), «Lo siento» (I'm sorry). «Lo siento» is a fixed phrase for apologizing — it isn't literally «I feel it». STEP 5: with «ser» and «estar», it's common to echo the adjective with «lo»: «¿Estás cansado? — Sí, lo estoy» (are you tired? —Yes, I am). That sounds more natural than the bare «Sí, estoy». STEP 6: verbs that commonly take a direct object: llamar, esperar, ayudar, visitar, invitar, acompañar, conocer, escuchar, mirar, buscar. STEP 7: «esperar» means both to wait for and to hope: «Te espero a las ocho» means «I'll wait for you at eight». «Buscar» means to look for or to go pick someone up: «Te busco en la estación» (I'll pick you up at the station). STEP 8: in Spain, for male people it's common to hear «le» instead of «lo» («le veo mañana»); this is called «leísmo», and it's accepted in Spain. This course uses «lo» and «la», and you'll be understood everywhere.
topicos.comparacao: English «I'll wait for you» and «call me» follow the same basic word order Spanish does for these forms, so «te espero» and «me llamas» feel familiar in structure. What has no real English counterpart is the neuter «lo»: English «I don't know» and «I understand» stand complete on their own, with nothing playing the role of an object, while Spanish prefers to anchor the idea to something with «lo sé» and «lo entiendo» — leaving it out isn't wrong exactly, but «lo» makes the sentence feel more complete and natural to a Spanish ear.

exemplos.ru: Te llamo esta noche, ¿vale?
exemplos.pt: I'll call you tonight, okay?

exemplos.ru: ¿Nos esperáis en la puerta?
exemplos.pt: Will you wait for us at the door?

exemplos.ru: No lo sé, pero lo busco ahora.
exemplos.pt: I don't know, but I'm looking into it now.

exemplos.ru: Lo siento mucho, llego tarde.
exemplos.pt: I'm sorry, I'm running late.

erros.motivo: The pronoun comes before the conjugated verb.
No hyphen, and it goes before the conjugated verb.
With «ayer», the verb goes in the indefinido: «llamaste».
With a male «usted», the pronoun is «lo».

topicos.titulo: Pronoun position and false friends
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: with «ir a + infinitive», «querer + infinitive», «poder + infinitive», there are two positions: «Voy a comprarlo» or «Lo voy a comprar»; «Puedo verla» or «La puedo ver». STEP 2: picking one position over the other is just a matter of style; both are correct. What you never do is put the pronoun in the middle: «Voy lo a comprar». STEP 3: with the pretérito perfecto, the pronoun never attaches to the participle: «Lo he visto», never «He visto-lo». STEP 4: for emphasis, the object gets repeated at the start of the sentence: «A Ana la vi ayer» (Ana, I saw her yesterday) and «Ese libro lo compré en Madrid» (that book, I bought it in Madrid). This is completely natural in both speech and writing. STEP 5: useful false friends for this lesson. «Cola» means a line of people (at a bank or a checkout): «Vi a Marta en la cola». It's also the word for glue and for an animal's tail. In several Latin American countries, like Mexico, «fila» is more common for a line of people; both are understood everywhere. «Oficina» means «office», not an auto repair shop (which is «taller»). «Pegar» means to hit or to glue, not «to catch» — for catching the bus, use «tomar».
topicos.comparacao: English keeps its object pronoun fixed after the verb no matter what else is going on in the sentence, so the idea that Spanish gives you two equally correct spots — before the whole verb phrase, or stuck onto the infinitive — is new territory, not a choice English makes you face. What never changes, in either language, is that the pronoun can't float in the middle of a verb phrase: English would never say «I'm going it to buy» any more than Spanish allows «Voy lo a comprar», so that instinct does transfer directly.

erros.certo: Voy a comprarlo. / Lo voy a comprar.
erros.motivo: The pronoun never sits in the middle of the verb group.
With the perfecto, the pronoun goes before «haber».
«Oficina» means office; an auto repair shop is «taller».

topicos.titulo: Le, les, and the other indirect object pronouns
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the indirect object answers the question «to whom?» or «for whom?» after the verb. In «Doy un libro a Ana», I give the book to whom? To Ana. The book is the direct object; Ana is the indirect object. STEP 2: the indirect object pronouns are «me» (me), «te» (you, tú), «le» (him, her, usted), «nos» (us), «os» (you-all, vosotros), and «les» (them, ustedes). Only the third person differs from the direct object of lesson 23: here it's «le, les», and there it was «lo, la, los, las». STEP 3: «le» and «les» don't change for gender: «Le doy un libro» works for «a ella» and for «a él». STEP 4: the position is the same as the direct object: before the conjugated verb («Le escribo») or attached to the infinitive («Quiero escribirle»). STEP 5: the pronoun shows up even when the person's name is also in the sentence: «Le doy el libro a Ana», «Les escribo a mis padres». That isn't redundancy — it's simply the normal way to speak. STEP 6: for emphasis or contrast, add «a mí», «a ti», «a él», «a ella», «a usted», «a nosotros», «a vosotros», «a ellos», «a ustedes»: «A mí me dio un libro y a ti no». STEP 7: an English speaker tends to translate "to her" literally and reach for just «a ella», leaving out the pronoun: «Dije a ella». The correct form always keeps the pronoun too: «le dije». STEP 8: the same pronouns show up with «gustar», which you've already seen: «A Ana le gusta el té» and «Me gusta el té».
topicos.comparacao: English marks the indirect object with word order instead of a required pronoun: «I gave her the book» or «I gave the book to her» both work, and the sentence is complete without any extra marker once "her" appears. Spanish never drops that marker: «le di el libro» keeps «le» in place even though «a ella» may also be stated outright, so the habit of skipping the pronoun once the person is already named — which feels natural in English — has to be unlearned for Spanish.

exemplos.ru: Le regalé un libro a mi hermana.
exemplos.pt: I gave my sister a book as a gift.

exemplos.ru: Les dije la verdad a mis padres.
exemplos.pt: I told my parents the truth.

exemplos.ru: Quiero mostrarte una foto.
exemplos.pt: I want to show you a photo.

exemplos.ru: ¿Me prestas el cargador?
exemplos.pt: Will you lend me the charger?

tabela.exemplo: Le explico la regla a Ana.

erros.motivo: In Spanish, the indirect object becomes a pronoun placed before the verb.
«Les» is only for plural; «mi madre» is singular.
The pronoun comes before the conjugated verb, with no hyphen.

erros.errado: Le doy los libros a mis amigos.
erros.certo: Les doy los libros a mis amigos.
erros.motivo: When the person is plural, the pronoun is plural too.

erros.errado: Yo dijo a ti la verdad.
erros.motivo: Use «te» for «a ti», and the form «dije» for «yo».

topicos.titulo: Direct or indirect, and false friends
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to decide between the two pronouns, ask the verb. "What? Whom?" points to the direct object («lo, la»). "To whom? For whom?" points to the indirect object («le, les»). «Escribí una carta» answers what was written; «Le escribí una carta» also answers to whom. STEP 2: verbs that almost always take an indirect object: dar, decir, escribir, contar, preguntar, responder, pedir, prestar, enseñar, ofrecer, regalar, explicar, mostrar, mandar, enviar, and also «gustar, interesar, encantar, doler, parecer». «Me duele la cabeza» (my head hurts — literally, the head hurts to me). STEP 3: verbs that take a direct object when it's a person: llamar, ayudar, esperar, visitar, invitar, escuchar, ver, conocer. «La llamo», «Lo ayudo». STEP 4: «preguntar» and «responder» take the indirect object, unlike how English sometimes treats them: «Le pregunté su nombre» and «Le respondí ayer» — English "I asked her" and "I answered him" look like direct objects, but Spanish treats the person as indirect here. STEP 5: «pedir» also takes the indirect object for the person being asked: «Le pedí un café al camarero». «Pedir prestado» means to borrow; «prestar» means to lend, not to render a service: «Le pedí prestado el coche» and «Le presté el coche». STEP 6: false friends: «apellido» is last name/surname, not nickname, which is «apodo» or «mote»: «Mi apellido es Rosa; mi apodo es Rosi». «Regalar» means to give as a gift, and «un regalo» is a gift — not a perk or a pleasure. «Pegar» means to hit or to glue, not to catch: «Le pegó a su hermano» means "he hit his brother". «Enseñar» means to teach and also to show: «Me enseñó su casa» means "he showed me his house". STEP 7: in Latin America, word order and the pronouns stay the same; what changes is «os», which doesn't exist there. Instead of «os escribo», you say «les escribo».
topicos.comparacao: English also keeps direct and indirect objects distinct in form sometimes («I saw her» versus «I gave her the book»), but everyday speech blurs the line by letting a single pronoun like "her" do double duty in both roles. Spanish keeps the split sharp no matter the context: «la vi» (direct) and «le di» (indirect) never swap. The false friends in this part can trip up an English speaker in a very specific way: «apellido» isn't close to a nickname, «prestar» has nothing to do with being "prestigious", and «pegar» has nothing to do with "pegging" something — it means to hit or stick.

tabela.exemplo: Mi apellido es Rosa, mi apodo es Rosi.

erros.motivo: «Preguntar» takes the indirect object for the person.
«Escribir algo a alguien» takes «le».

erros.errado: Mi apellido es Pepe. (meaning to say: nickname)
erros.motivo: «Apellido» means last name; the nickname is «apodo».

erros.errado: Pegué el coche a mi hermano. (meaning to say: I lent)
erros.certo: Le presté el coche a mi hermano.
erros.motivo: «Pegar» means to hit or to glue; to lend is «prestar».
The pronoun comes before the verb.

topicos.titulo: Asking and offering with «me», and clarifying «le»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to ask for something politely, use «me» with an action verb: «¿Me trae la cuenta?», «¿Me pone un café?», «¿Me puede ayudar?». The «me» marks that the request is for you. STEP 2: to offer, use «te» or «le»: «¿Te ayudo?», «¿Le ayudo, señora?», «¿Le pongo algo más?». STEP 3: with «usted», «le» doesn't say the gender. If you need to, clarify: «Le dije a usted, no a ella». STEP 4: to clarify an ambiguous «le», add «a + person»: «Le escribí a Marta», «Les mandamos una invitación a sus padres». STEP 5: with the verb «contestar», the indirect object is the person: «Le contesté a Ana» (I answered Ana). To answer the phone, you say «contestar el teléfono». STEP 6: in the indefinido, the forms are the usual ones, with the pronoun in front: «Le di», «Le dije», «Le escribí», «Nos mandaron».
topicos.comparacao: English politeness formulas like "could you bring me the check?" and "can I help you?" put the pronoun in roughly the same spot Spanish does, so the basic shape transfers fine. What doesn't transfer is that Spanish courtesy phrasing is more direct about who's asking: «¿Le ayudo?» to a customer, «¿Me trae la cuenta?» to a waiter — there's no softening "would you mind" built into the grammar the way English speakers often add one.

tabela.frase: Le escribí a Marta, no a su hermana.

erros.motivo: The pronoun attaches to the infinitive with no hyphen.
With «tú», use «te»; «le» is for «usted».

erros.errado: Le dije a usted, no ella.
erros.certo: Le dije a usted, no a ella.
erros.motivo: The «a» can't be left out before the person.

topicos.titulo: Indirect object + direct object: pronoun order
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: a sentence can have both complements: «Doy el libro a Ana». The book is the direct object (what?) and Ana is the indirect object (to whom?). If you swap both for pronouns, the sentence becomes «Se lo doy». STEP 2: there's just one rule: the person pronoun (the indirect one) comes first, then the thing pronoun (the direct one). In other words, «me, te, nos, os» come before «lo, la, los, las». STEP 3: «¿Me das el libro? — Sí, te lo doy». Here «te» is the person I'm giving it to (you) and «lo» is «el libro». STEP 4: nothing goes between the two pronouns, and they never flip order: «me lo», never «lo me». STEP 5: «lo, la, los, las» agree with the thing, not the person. A feminine plural thing is always «las», whoever the person is: «Me las das», «Te las doy». STEP 6: the position is the usual one, before the conjugated verb: «Me lo dices», «No te lo digo», «Nos las trae». STEP 7: in the compound tenses, both pronouns go before «haber»: «Te lo he dicho». In the indefinido: «Me lo dio», «Te la mandé». STEP 8: English doesn't have a contracted double-pronoun form either, but it solves the same two-pronoun problem differently: when both the person and the thing are pronouns, English usually needs "to" — "I'll give it to you" — rather than stacking two bare pronouns the way Spanish does.
topicos.comparacao: Some English speakers do say "give me it" or "give it me" in certain dialects, but it's regional and never the safe default; the standard form keeps the preposition. Spanish's «me lo», «te la» pattern — person-pronoun immediately before thing-pronoun, with no preposition at all — has no everyday English equivalent, so it takes real practice before it feels automatic. This combination, used constantly in everyday Spanish, is one of the biggest new habits at this level.

exemplos.ru: ¿Me prestas el cargador? — Sí, te lo presto.
exemplos.pt: Will you lend me the charger? Yes, I'll lend it to you.

exemplos.ru: Quiero ver las entradas. — Ahora te las traigo.
exemplos.pt: I want to see the tickets. I'll bring them to you now.

exemplos.ru: Nos explican la regla y nos la repiten.
exemplos.pt: They explain the rule to us and repeat it for us.

erros.motivo: The pronoun comes before the verb, and the indirect one comes first.
The order is always indirect first (me, te, nos, os), then direct (lo, la, los, las).

erros.errado: Te los doy. (meaning to say: the key)
erros.motivo: The direct pronoun agrees with the thing: «la llave» is feminine singular.
The pronoun never sits between the auxiliary and the participle.

topicos.titulo: Se lo: when the indirect object is «le» or «les»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: if the indirect object is third-person («le, les») and the direct one is «lo, la, los, las», a sound clash comes up: «le lo», «les la». Spanish avoids this by swapping «le» and «les» for «se». STEP 2: «Le doy el libro a Ana» becomes «Se lo doy». «Les mando las entradas a mis padres» becomes «Se las mando». STEP 3: this «se» is not the reflexive «se». It's «le» or «les» transformed, so it doesn't say whether the person is one or several, or male or female — the listener works that out from context. STEP 4: «lo, la, los, las» agree with the thing: «Les di las llaves» becomes «Se las di», and «las» is for «llaves», not for whoever received them. STEP 5: to clarify who, add «a + person» at the end: «Se lo di a Ana», «Se las mandé a mis padres», «Se lo dije a usted». STEP 6: with the infinitive, both pronouns attach to the end: «dar + se + lo» becomes «dárselo». Since the word grows longer, you must write the accent on the original stressed syllable: «dárselo, decírtelo, mostrárselo, comprármelo, escribírselo». STEP 7: as in other cases, there are two positions: «Voy a dárselo» or «Se lo voy a dar». STEP 8: in Latin America, «os» doesn't exist: instead of «os lo digo», you say «se lo digo» for «ustedes». STEP 9: a false friend in this part: «dirección» means address (and also direction): «¿Me das tu dirección?». Email is «correo» or «correo electrónico».
topicos.comparacao: English has nothing like the «se» substitution either, because English never runs into the same clash in the first place — it keeps the preposition, so «I gave it to him» never risks stacking two colliding third-person pronouns. Treat Spanish «se lo», «se la» as a dedicated rule to memorize rather than a translation of anything already in your English habits, and don't confuse this «se» with the reflexive «se» of «se lava» or the impersonal «se» of «se habla español» — they look identical but do something completely different.

exemplos.ru: ¿Le dijiste la verdad a Marta? — Sí, se la dije.
exemplos.pt: Did you tell Marta the truth? Yes, I told it to her.

exemplos.ru: ¿Cuándo les mandas las fotos? — Se las mando hoy.
exemplos.pt: When are you sending them the photos? I'm sending them today.

exemplos.ru: Quiero decírtelo ahora.
exemplos.pt: I want to tell you that now.

exemplos.ru: El camarero nos trajo la cuenta y se la pagamos.
exemplos.pt: The waiter brought us the check and we paid it to him.

tabela.frase_completa: Le doy el libro a Ana.
Le mando la carta a Pablo.
Les di los billetes a mis padres.
Les expliqué las reglas a los niños.
Voy a dar el regalo a Marta.
tabela.com_pronomes: Voy a dárselo. / Se lo voy a dar.

erros.motivo: «Le lo» doesn't exist; use «se lo».

erros.errado: Les las mandé a mis padres.
erros.certo: Se las mandé a mis padres.
erros.motivo: «Les las» doesn't exist; use «se las».

erros.errado: Se la di a mis padres. (the keys)
erros.certo: Se las di a mis padres.
erros.motivo: The direct pronoun agrees with the thing: «las llaves».
With two pronouns attached to the infinitive, the written accent is required.
With «ustedes», the pronoun is «se», not «os».

topicos.titulo: Reflexive + direct object, and vocabulary from Spain and Latin America
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the reflexive verbs from lesson 14 can also take a direct object: «Me pongo la chaqueta», «Me lavo las manos». When the direct object becomes a pronoun, the reflexive comes first: «Me la pongo», «Me las lavo». STEP 2: with the third person, the reflexive «se» comes before «lo»: «Se puso el abrigo» becomes «Se lo puso». STEP 3: asking for something with two pronouns feels natural: «¿Me lo puedes explicar?», «¿Puedes explicármelo?». STEP 4: vocabulary differs between Spain and Latin America. «Móvil», «ordenador», «coche», and «billete» (Spain) correspond to «celular», «computadora», «carro», and «boleto» or «pasaje» (many Latin American countries). Both are understood everywhere; hearing the other one shouldn't come as a surprise. STEP 5: use the variant from your target region and stay consistent. In this course, the audio is from Spain, and the Latin American words are given as a note.
topicos.comparacao: English also lets a reflexive and a direct object show up together ("he put on his coat" → "he put it on"), and the pronoun order mirrors Spanish's: the thing-pronoun slots in where the noun was. What's new isn't the order so much as the habit — Spanish keeps doing this constantly in everyday speech («se lo puso»), where English just as often skips the pronoun and repeats the noun or rephrases instead.

tabela.frase: Me voy a poner el abrigo.
tabela.com_pronome: Me lo voy a poner. / Voy a ponérmelo.

erros.motivo: The pronoun comes before the verb, with no hyphen.
With two pronouns attached to the infinitive, the accent is required.
The reflexive comes first, then the direct object.

topicos.titulo: Comparing with «más… que», «menos… que», and «tan… como»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to say something has more of a quality than something else, use «más» + adjective + «que»: «El tren es más rápido que el autobús.» STEP 2: to say it has less, swap «más» for «menos»: «El autobús es menos caro que el tren.» STEP 3: to say two things are equal, use «tan» + adjective + «como»: «Mi hermana es tan alta como yo.» «Tan» never changes — not for gender, not for number. STEP 4: the adjective agrees with what's being described, not with «más»: «Ana es más alta que Pablo», «Los pisos son más caros que las casas». STEP 5: after «que» and «como», use the subject pronoun: «Soy más alto que tú», «Es tan lento como yo» — never «que ti» or «como mí». English casual speech often says "taller than me," but the strict grammar rule you were taught — "taller than I (am)" — is the one that actually matches Spanish here, with no exception. STEP 6: with nouns, equality uses «tanto, tanta, tantos, tantas» + noun + «como», and «tanto» agrees with the noun: «Tengo tantos libros como tú», «Hay tanta gente como ayer». STEP 7: with verbs, use «tanto como» with no changes: «Trabajo tanto como tú.» STEP 8: other ways to say "the same": «igual de + adjective + que»: «Es igual de difícil que el otro», and «el mismo, la misma… que»: «Tengo el mismo móvil que tú.» STEP 9: use «más de» + number, never «más que»: «Hay más de veinte personas.» «Que» only shows up when comparing two things: «Hay más gente que ayer.»
topicos.comparacao: English often builds the comparative with the suffix "-er" on short adjectives (faster, cheaper) instead of a separate word, while Spanish never has a suffix for this — it's always «más/menos + adjective + que», with no exception for short words. The equality pattern lines up well: «tan alto como» is just "as tall as." The real trap is the pronoun after «que»: English speakers who say "taller than me" in everyday speech need the formal "than I" instinct here, since Spanish allows no informal shortcut — «que tú», «que yo», never «que ti», «que mí».

exemplos.ru: El examen es más fácil que el del año pasado.
exemplos.pt: The test is easier than last year's.

exemplos.ru: Este móvil es menos caro que aquel.
exemplos.pt: This phone is cheaper than that one.

exemplos.ru: Ella habla tan rápido como su madre.
exemplos.pt: She talks as fast as her mother.

exemplos.ru: Hay más de treinta alumnos en la clase.
exemplos.pt: There are more than thirty students in the class.

linhas.exemplo: Este bolso es más caro que ese.
Esta calle es menos ruidosa que la otra.
Mi hermano es tan alto como mi padre.

erros.motivo: Between two things being compared, use «que»; «de» only ever comes before a number.
Before a number, Spanish uses «más de».

erros.errado: Ella es tan alta que yo.
erros.certo: Ella es tan alta como yo.
erros.motivo: Equality is «tan… como», never «tan… que».
«Tanto» agrees with the noun: tantos libros.

topicos.titulo: Mejor, peor, mayor, and menor
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: four adjectives have their own comparative and skip «más» entirely: «bueno» becomes «mejor» (better), «malo» becomes «peor» (worse), «grande» can become «mayor», and «pequeño» can become «menor». STEP 2: «mejor» and «peor» are the ones you'll use most. You say «Este restaurante es mejor que ese», never «más bueno que ese». Same with «malo»: «Hoy el tiempo es peor que ayer». STEP 3: «mejor» and «peor» also work as adverbs, meaning "better" and "worse" with a verb: «Hablas mejor que yo», «Hoy canto peor». STEP 4: «mayor» and «menor» talk about age or importance: «mi hermano mayor» is the older brother, «mi hermana menor» is the younger sister, «un problema mayor» is a bigger problem. For physical size, use «más grande» and «más pequeño»: «Mi casa es más grande que la tuya.» English's own irregular comparatives — good→better, bad→worse — line up neatly with «mejor» and «peor», but English "older" and "younger" are perfectly regular, so «mayor» and «menor» being irregular here is new, not something you can lean on from English. STEP 5: the plurals are «mejores, peores, mayores, menores» — no accent mark, no gender change: «Estas fotos son mejores que aquellas.» STEP 6: for quantity, use «más» and «menos», which are already comparatives and don't change: «Tengo más tiempo que tú», «Come menos que yo». STEP 7: with «mayor», the phrase «una persona mayor» is a polite way to say an elderly person. STEP 8: you can strengthen a comparative with «mucho» or «bastante»: «mucho mejor», «bastante más caro». Never say «muy más» or «muy mejor».
topicos.comparacao: English also has its own irregular comparatives for "good" and "bad" — better, worse — so «mejor» and «peor» feel familiar right away. What doesn't carry over is «mayor» and «menor»: English "older" and "younger" are built the regular way, with no irregular form at all, so there's nothing in English to anchor these two to — and the fact that Spanish «mayor»/«menor» lean toward age and importance rather than physical size (which still takes «más grande»/«más pequeño») is a split English doesn't make either.

exemplos.ru: Tu español es mejor que el mío.
exemplos.pt: Your Spanish is better than mine.

exemplos.ru: Esta película es mucho peor que la otra.
exemplos.pt: This movie is a lot worse than the other one.

exemplos.ru: Mi hermano mayor tiene treinta años.
exemplos.pt: My older brother is thirty.

exemplos.ru: Tu casa es más grande que la mía.
exemplos.pt: Your house is bigger than mine.

linhas.exemplo: El pan de aquí es mejor.
Mi hermano mayor vive en Bilbao.

erros.errado: Este café es más bueno que ese.
erros.certo: Este café es mejor que ese.
erros.motivo: «Bueno» has its own comparative: «mejor».

erros.errado: Hoy estoy más malo que ayer.
erros.motivo: «Malo» becomes «peor».

erros.errado: Mi casa es mayor que la tuya. (size)
erros.certo: Mi casa es más grande que la tuya.
erros.motivo: For physical size use «más grande»; «mayor» is about age or importance.
Before a comparative, use «mucho», never «muy».

topicos.titulo: The superlative: «el más… de» and «-ísimo»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to say something is the maximum within a group, put the article before «más» or «menos»: «Madrid es la ciudad más grande de España.» The structure is «el, la, los, las» + (noun) + «más» + adjective + «de» + the group. STEP 2: after the group, use «de», never "in": «el más alto de la clase», «la más cara de la tienda». STEP 3: with «mejor» and «peor», the article comes right before them: «el mejor restaurante de la ciudad», «la peor idea del día». STEP 4: without a group, the article changes the meaning: «Es más caro» (comparison) versus «Es el más caro» (superlative). STEP 5: the other superlative is the absolute one: saying a quality is very intense. You form it with «muy» + adjective («muy caro») or with the ending «-ísimo, -ísima»: «carísimo», «riquísimo», «facilísimo». Drop the final vowel of the adjective and add «-ísimo»: «caro → carísimo», «grande → grandísimo». English has no suffix of its own for this absolute superlative — it just stacks on "very" or "extremely" — so «-ísimo» is a genuinely new tool, not a translation of anything you already do with adjectives. STEP 6: small spelling changes keep the sound the same: «rico → riquísimo» (c becomes qu), «largo → larguísimo» (g becomes gu), «feliz → felicísimo» (z becomes c). STEP 7: false friend: «largo» means long, not "large" — despite looking exactly like the English word. The opposite of «estrecho» (narrow) is «ancho» (wide): «una calle ancha», «un río largo».
topicos.comparacao: The relative superlative lines up closely with English: "the most expensive city in Spain" is «la ciudad más caro de España», just swapping "in" for «de». The absolute superlative is where English has nothing to offer: there's no English suffix that does what «-ísimo» does, so «carísimo» and «facilísimo» are a new pattern to build, not a translation of an existing one. And «largo» is a trap specifically for an English speaker, since it looks exactly like "large" but actually means "long" — the real word for large/wide is «ancho».

exemplos.ru: Es la calle más ruidosa de mi barrio.
exemplos.pt: It's the noisiest street in my neighborhood.

exemplos.ru: Este es el mejor pueblo de la región.
exemplos.pt: This is the best town in the region.

exemplos.ru: El examen fue facilísimo.
exemplos.pt: The test was super easy.

exemplos.ru: Es un río larguísimo.
exemplos.pt: It's an extremely long river.

erros.errado: Es la ciudad más grande en España.
erros.certo: Es la ciudad más grande de España.
erros.motivo: After the group, Spanish uses «de».
«Mejor» is already a comparative: it never takes «más».

erros.errado: Es una calle larga. (meaning to say wide)
erros.motivo: «Largo» means long; for width, use «ancho».
To keep the "k" sound, «c» becomes «qu».

topicos.titulo: The regular simple future
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the simple future is built from the whole infinitive — nothing gets dropped. That holds for all three groups (-ar, -er, -ir): «hablar», «comer», «vivir». STEP 2: add these endings to the infinitive: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án. They're the same for all three groups. «Hablaré, hablarás, hablará, hablaremos, hablaréis, hablarán.» STEP 3: every form carries an accent except «nosotros»: «hablaré», «hablarás», «hablará», «hablaremos», «hablaréis», «hablarán». STEP 4: the pronoun «yo» and the others are usually dropped; the ending already tells you who. STEP 5: for the nearer future, everyday speech prefers the present or «ir a + infinitive» (lesson 30): «Mañana trabajo», «Mañana voy a trabajar». The simple future sounds firmer or more formal and shows up a lot in predictions, promises, and written text. STEP 6: uses of the future: plans («El año que viene estudiaré en Granada»), predictions («Mañana lloverá»), promises («Te llamaré esta noche»), and probability about the present («Serán las cinco», meaning "it must be five o'clock"). STEP 7: the future with «si» and the present: «Si estudias, aprobarás», with the present after «si». The future never follows «si»: you don't say «si estudiarás».
topicos.comparacao: English has no built-in future tense form at all — it just drops "will" in front of the unchanged infinitive for every single person: "I will speak, you will speak, she will speak." There's no ending to memorize and no distinction by person or number. Spanish's future really is a tacked-on suffix on the full infinitive (-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án), which means six different endings to learn where English gets by with one invariant word. Don't forget the accent either: without it, «hablara» is a completely different verb form, not the future.

exemplos.ru: El año que viene viviré en Valencia.
exemplos.pt: Next year I'm going to live in Valencia.

exemplos.ru: Mañana te llamaré por la noche.
exemplos.pt: I'll call you tonight.

exemplos.ru: La semana que viene comeremos con mis padres.
exemplos.pt: Next week we're having lunch with my parents.

exemplos.ru: ¿Dónde estarán mis llaves?
exemplos.pt: I wonder where my keys are. (I'm asking myself)

erros.motivo: The future keeps the whole infinitive: hablar + ás.
After «si», use the present, never the future.

erros.errado: Yo hablaré, tú hablarás, él hablara.
erros.certo: Yo hablaré, tú hablarás, él hablará.
erros.motivo: The «él» form takes an accent: «hablará».
The «nosotros» ending is «-emos» for all three groups.

topicos.titulo: Ten verbs that change the stem in the future
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: some common verbs don't use the whole infinitive. But the endings are the usual ones: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án. STEP 2: the first group drops the infinitive's vowel: «poder → podré», «saber → sabré», «querer → querré», «haber → habré». STEP 3: the second group swaps the vowel for a «d»: «tener → tendré», «venir → vendré», «poner → pondré», «salir → saldré». STEP 4: the third group is the most irregular, since it drops letters: «decir → diré», «hacer → haré». STEP 5: the verbs built from these follow the base verb: «contener → contendré», «mantener → mantendré», «deshacer → desharé». STEP 6: «haber» in the future shows up almost only as «habrá» (there will be), an impersonal form that's always singular: «Mañana habrá una fiesta», «Habrá muchas personas». STEP 7: the future gets used a lot with «querer» and «poder» in careful speech: «¿Podrás venir?», «No querrá hablar». STEP 8: every other verb is regular in the future, including the ones that are irregular in the present: «ir → iré», «ser → seré», «estar → estaré», «dar → daré», «ver → veré». Memorize the ten: tendré, haré, diré, podré, pondré, saldré, vendré, sabré, querré, habré.
topicos.comparacao: English has nothing resembling a sound change here, since "will" never touches the verb at all — "will have," "will do," "will come" stay exactly as regular as any other verb after "will." So these ten changed stems aren't a pattern you can borrow from English; they're ten forms to simply memorize as a set, the same way you'd memorize an irregular past tense, just in a different slot.

exemplos.ru: Mañana tendré una reunión importante.
exemplos.pt: Tomorrow I'll have an important meeting.

exemplos.ru: El sábado saldremos con unos amigos.
exemplos.pt: On Saturday we'll go out with some friends.

exemplos.ru: Te diré la verdad cuando vengas.
exemplos.pt: I'll tell you the truth when you get here.

exemplos.ru: El viernes habrá una fiesta en el barrio.
exemplos.pt: On Friday there will be a party in the neighborhood.

erros.motivo: The stem of «tener» in the future is «tendr-».
«Hacer» drops the «ce»: haré, harás…
Use just one verb; «venir» in the future is «vendr-».
The future of «salir» is «saldr-».

topicos.titulo: What the future is for: predictions, promises, and guesses
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: prediction: the future describes what's expected to happen. «Mañana lloverá en el norte», «La semana que viene hará más frío». STEP 2: promise and firm decision: «Te lo prometo: estudiaré todos los días», «Mañana te llamaré». STEP 3: a soft command with a note of authority: «Mañana vendrás a las nueve», which isn't a question but a heads-up that barely leaves room to say no. Use it carefully. STEP 4: doubt or guessing about the present: «¿Dónde estará Ana?» (I wonder where Ana is) and «Estará en casa» (She must be home). This only works with the simple future. English actually does something similar with "will": "She'll be home by now" works as a guess about the present the same way «Estará en casa» does — so this particular use transfers more naturally than most of this lesson. STEP 5: use time markers to place the action: «mañana», «el año que viene», «dentro de una semana». «Dentro de» means "in," the same "in" as English "in an hour": «Llegaré dentro de una hora» is "I'll arrive in an hour." STEP 6: «en una hora» can also mean the same thing, but «dentro de» is the clearer choice. STEP 7: with «cuando» and the future, Spanish uses the present (subjunctive) in the «cuando» clause: «Cuando llegues, te llamaré» — you'll see why later; for now just learn the pattern as a fixed phrase. STEP 8: weather talk: «llover» (llueve, lloverá), «hacer sol / calor / frío / viento», «estar nublado».
topicos.comparacao: English predictions use "it's going to rain" or "it will rain" about as interchangeably as Spanish uses «va a llover» and «lloverá», so that part feels familiar. The real overlap worth noticing is the guessing use: English "he'll be tired" or "that'll be John" works the same way as «estará cansado» — both languages reach for the future tense to mark a confident guess, not just something scheduled to happen.

tabela.traducao: It will rain in Galicia tomorrow.
I'll call you tonight.

tabela.exemplo: El año que viene estudiaré inglés.
tabela.traducao: Next year I'm going to study English.
It must be five o'clock.
Chego daqui a uma hora.

erros.motivo: The full expression is «dentro de».
After «si», use the present.
The impersonal «haber» stays singular, even with a plural.

erros.errado: Estará muy cansado. (meaning "he's tired, I'm sure")
erros.motivo: The future of guessing signals doubt; for a plain fact, use the present.

topicos.titulo: The affirmative imperative of tú and usted
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the imperative is used to give an instruction, ask for something, invite, or give advice: «Mira», «Escucha», «Pasa». STEP 2: for «tú», the affirmative form is the same as the «él, ella» present-tense form. «Habla» (from hablar), «come» (from comer), «escribe» (from escribir). English's whole imperative, by contrast, is just the bare infinitive with no subject at all — "Look," "Listen," "Wait" — the same single form whether you're talking to one person, several people, a friend, or a stranger. Spanish's split between «tú» and «usted» forms, and the eight irregular «tú» forms coming up next, have no counterpart in English's one-size-fits-all imperative. STEP 3: verbs that change the stem vowel in the present do the same in the imperative: «cierra» (from cerrar), «vuelve» (from volver), «pide» (from pedir), «sigue» (from seguir). STEP 4: eight verbs have an irregular «tú» imperative, and you just have to memorize them: venir → «ven», decir → «di», hacer → «haz», ir → «ve», poner → «pon», salir → «sal», ser → «sé», tener → «ten». STEP 5: for «usted», you don't use the present-tense form; you use the present subjunctive. As a shortcut, just switch the ending's vowel. -ar verbs end in -e instead: «hable», «mire», «espere». -er and -ir verbs end in -a instead: «coma», «escriba», «abra». STEP 6: the «usted» irregulars follow the «yo» present: «venga», «diga», «haga», «vaya», «ponga», «salga», «sea», «tenga». STEP 7: for «ustedes» (more than one person), add «-n»: «hablen», «coman», «escriban». STEP 8: pronouns go after the verb and attach to it: «Escúchame», «Dime», «Siéntate». When you attach the pronoun, the written accent keeps the stress where it was: «escucha → escúchame», «cierra → ciérrala». STEP 9: the imperative only needs «por favor» to sound polite: «Pasa, por favor», «Espere un momento, por favor».
topicos.comparacao: Pronoun attachment is the other piece with no English parallel: English "listen to me" or "sit down" never attaches a pronoun onto the verb itself or shifts its stress — the pronoun is just a separate word that comes after, same as everywhere else in English. Spanish gluing «me» onto «escucha» to make «escúchame», with an added accent mark to keep the stress in place, is a mechanic you'll have to build from scratch.

exemplos.ru: Mira, esa es mi calle.
exemplos.pt: Look, this is my street.

exemplos.ru: Pasa, por favor, y siéntate.
exemplos.pt: Come in, please, and sit down.

exemplos.ru: Espere un momento, por favor.
exemplos.pt: Wait a moment, please.

exemplos.ru: Ten cuidado con el escalón.
exemplos.pt: Watch the step.

erros.motivo: «Viene» is the present of «él»; the «tú» imperative of «venir» is «ven».
The imperative of «hacer» is «haz», not «hace».
The imperative of «decir» is «di».
With «usted», use the subjunctive form: «hable».

topicos.titulo: The negative imperative: «no» + subjunctive
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to negate a command, the «tú» form changes: you don't use the affirmative imperative. You write «no» + the present subjunctive form: «no hables», «no comas», «no escribas». STEP 2: how it's formed: -ar verbs swap «-as» for «-es», and -er and -ir verbs swap «-es» for «-as». Start from the «tú» present form: hablas → hables; comes → comas; escribes → escribas. This is new ground for an English speaker: English's negative imperative is just "don't" + the exact same bare infinitive you'd use affirmatively — "don't talk," "don't eat" — with no vowel swap and no subjunctive at all. STEP 3: with «usted» and «ustedes», the negative form is the same as the affirmative, with «no» in front: «no hable», «no coma», «no hablen». STEP 4: with «vosotros» (Spain), the affirmative is formed by swapping the infinitive's final «-r» for «-d»: «hablad», «comed», «escribid». The negative is «no» + subjunctive: «no habléis», «no comáis», «no escribáis». STEP 5: «ir» is the only exception to the «vosotros» affirmative: «id». STEP 6: in reflexive verbs, «vosotros» drops the «-d» before «-os»: «sentaos», «levantaos». STEP 7: the «tú» negative irregulars follow the «yo» present: «no digas», «no hagas», «no vayas», «no pongas», «no salgas», «no seas», «no tengas», «no vengas». STEP 8: in the negative, pronouns go before the verb, as separate words: «no me llames», «no te levantes», «no lo hagas». In the affirmative, they go after and attach: «llámame», «levántate», «hazlo».
topicos.comparacao: English pronoun position never flips between affirmative and negative — "call me" and "don't call me" both keep the pronoun as its own word right after the verb. Spanish's switch — attached after the verb in the affirmative («llámame»), a separate word before the verb in the negative («no me llames») — is a genuinely new rule to track, on top of the subjunctive switch itself.

exemplos.ru: No hables tan rápido, por favor.
exemplos.pt: Don't talk so fast, please.

exemplos.ru: No me llames después de las diez.
exemplos.pt: Don't call me after ten.

exemplos.ru: No vayas solo por esa calle.
exemplos.pt: Don't go alone down that street.

exemplos.ru: Venid pronto y no lleguéis tarde.
exemplos.pt: Come soon and don't arrive late. (Spain)

tabelas.titulo: Affirmative and negative tú, side by side

erros.errado: No habla tan rápido. (order to a friend)
erros.motivo: In a negative order to «tú», use the subjunctive, not the affirmative form.
Negative order: «no» + subjunctive.
In the affirmative, the pronoun comes after the verb and attaches to it.

erros.errado: Me llama más tarde. (as a command)
erros.motivo: In the affirmative, the pronoun goes after and attaches: «llámame».

topicos.titulo: Instructions, invitations, notices, and courtesy
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: step-by-step instructions (recipes, manuals) use the «tú» or «usted» imperative, in short sentences: «Corta las patatas», «Fríe el huevo». STEP 2: asking for something: the imperative with «por favor» is correct, but a question is often preferred to sound friendlier: «¿Puedes cerrar la puerta?» instead of «Cierra la puerta». STEP 3: inviting: the imperative is warm here, not a command: «Pasa», «Siéntate», «Come un poco más». STEP 4: words to get someone's attention in formal settings: «oiga» (excuse me, with «usted»), «perdone» or «disculpe» (sorry/excuse me), and «mire» (look). STEP 5: on signs and notices, the infinitive is used instead of the imperative: «Empujar», «Tirar», «No fumar», «Cerrar la puerta» — a genuinely different habit from English, which puts signs in the imperative too ("Push," "Pull," "No smoking") but Spanish prefers the plain infinitive form. STEP 6: watch two confusing look-alikes: «ve» is the imperative of «ir» («Ve a casa») and also of «ver» («Ve esta película»); context sorts it out. And «sal» is the imperative of «salir» («Sal ahora») and also means table salt. STEP 7: in Spain, «coge» (from coger) means "grab/catch," but in parts of Latin America the verb has a vulgar sense; to be safe everywhere, use «toma» or «agarra» instead. And remember that «pegar» in Spanish means to hit or to glue — never "to grab" or "to catch," even though it might look like it should. STEP 8: with «ustedes», the imperative works for any group: «Pasen, por favor.» In Spain, among friends, it's «Pasad».
topicos.comparacao: English also uses the imperative on signs ("Push," "No smoking"), so that habit transfers fine — Spanish's preference for the bare infinitive instead («Empujar», «No fumar») is the one adjustment to make. The real trap is «pegar», which looks close enough to "peg" or could be mistaken for "to grab" — it actually means to hit or to glue. To say "grab it," reach for «toma» or «agarra» instead.

tabela.exemplo: Corta las patatas en trozos pequeños.
tabela.traducao: Cut the potatoes into small pieces.
Close the door, please.
Come in and sit down.
Excuse me, where's the bathroom?
Proibido fumar.

erros.motivo: «Pegar» means to hit or to glue; for "grab," use «tomar».
Signs and notices usually use the infinitive.
With a stranger, use «usted»: «disculpe».
The imperative «ve» carries no accent (but «sé», from «ser», does).

topicos.titulo: The simple conditional: forms
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: among other things, the conditional is used to ask, advise, and wish politely. The forms are easy to learn because they follow the future. STEP 2: take the whole infinitive (just like the future): «hablar», «comer», «vivir». STEP 3: add the conditional endings: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. They're the same for all three groups. «Hablaría, hablarías, hablaría, hablaríamos, hablaríais, hablarían.» All of them carry an accent on the «í». English has nothing like this ending system — its conditional is just "would" + the bare verb, the same for every single person, no suffix at all: "I would speak, you would speak, she would speak." Just like with the future, Spanish's six endings are new work, not a shortcut from anything in English. STEP 4: the ten irregular future verbs keep the same irregular stem in the conditional: «tendr-», «har-», «dir-», «podr-», «pondr-», «saldr-», «vendr-», «sabr-», «querr-», «habr-». Just change the ending: «tendría», «haría», «diría», «podría», «pondría», «saldría», «vendría», «sabría», «querría», «habría». STEP 5: every other verb is regular: «ser → sería», «ir → iría», «estar → estaría», «dar → daría», «ver → vería». STEP 6: the most common courtesy verb is «poder»: «¿Podría ayudarme?», «¿Podrías abrir la ventana?». STEP 7: the other two are «gustar» and «querer»: «Me gustaría un café», «Querría hablar con usted». «Gustaría» takes an indirect object pronoun, just like «gusta» (lesson 16): «Me gustaría», «Te gustaría», «Le gustaría». STEP 8: «quisiera» (lesson 8) is another courtesy form. It belongs to a tense called the subjunctive, which we'll get to later; for now, just use it as a set phrase: «Quisiera un café». «Querría» and «quisiera» are equivalent here. STEP 9: object pronouns go before the conjugated verb, or attached to the infinitive: «¿Me podría ayudar?» and «¿Podría ayudarme?» are both correct.
topicos.comparacao: Spanish's conditional ending really is a suffix tacked onto the full infinitive (or the same irregular stem the future uses), which means building a whole new ending set, the way the future did — English's single invariant "would" offers no shortcut here. What does echo something familiar is the courtesy use itself: English "would" softens requests the same way («Could you help me?», «I would like a coffee»), so the function is instantly recognizable even if the grammar underneath isn't.

exemplos.ru: ¿Podría ayudarme, por favor?
exemplos.pt: Could you help me, please?

exemplos.ru: Me gustaría un café con leche.
exemplos.pt: I would like a coffee with milk.

exemplos.ru: Querría hablar con la directora.
exemplos.pt: I would like to speak with the director.

exemplos.ru: ¿Te importaría cerrar la ventana?
exemplos.pt: Would you mind closing the window?

erros.motivo: The irregular stem of «tener» is «tendr-».
The ending carries an accent on the «í».
The conditional always has an accent on the «í».
With «con» and «tú», the form is «contigo».

topicos.titulo: Advising, suggesting, and wishing
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to give advice gently, use the conditional of «deber» and «poder»: «Deberías dormir más», «Podrías hablar con tu jefa». The conditional softens the advice; «Debes dormir más» sounds like an order. STEP 2: the formula «Yo que tú» + conditional is very common: «Yo que tú, hablaría con ella», meaning "if I were you, I'd talk to her." There's also «En tu lugar» + conditional: «En tu lugar, no iría». STEP 3: with «usted», the formula changes: «Yo que usted, esperaría» or «En su lugar, esperaría». STEP 4: «sería mejor» + infinitive, or «sería mejor que» + subjunctive (coming later): «Sería mejor salir pronto». STEP 5: to express a wish, use «Me gustaría», «Me encantaría» (I'd love to), «Querría»: «Me encantaría conocer Sevilla.» STEP 6: the conditional also marks politeness when asking for information: «¿Sabría decirme dónde está la estación?» (Would you happen to know where the station is?). STEP 7: don't use the conditional to give an order. For a request among friends, the present is just as natural: «¿Me pasas la sal?» Use the conditional when you want to be more careful, or with people you don't know. STEP 8: don't mix up these two verbs: «pedir» means to request or order something («Te pido un favor», «Pido un café»), and «preguntar» means to ask a question («Te pregunto una cosa»). Someone requesting something doesn't use «por»: the object comes straight after, «pedir un café».
topicos.comparacao: English runs on the exact same two formulas: "You should rest more" softens the same way «Deberías» does compared to the blunter "You must rest," and "If I were you, I'd talk to her" matches «Yo que tú, hablaría con ella» almost word for word. This whole lesson's logic transfers cleanly — the harder part is just remembering that «pedir» and «preguntar» split what English's single verb "to ask" covers, so you have to pick the right one every time English wouldn't force you to.

exemplos.ru: Deberías descansar un poco.
exemplos.pt: You should rest a little.

exemplos.ru: Yo en tu lugar, no compraría ese móvil.
exemplos.pt: In your place, I wouldn't buy that phone.

exemplos.ru: Me encantaría ir a Granada contigo.
exemplos.pt: I'd love to go to Granada with you.

exemplos.ru: Sería mejor llegar antes de las nueve.
exemplos.pt: It would be better to arrive before nine.

tabela.traducao: Você deveria dormir mais.

tabela.exemplo: Yo que tú, hablaría con ella.
tabela.traducao: Se eu fosse você, falaria com ela.
I'd love to see Seville.
Would you happen to know where the station is?

tabela.exemplo: Te pido un favor. / Te pregunto una cosa.
tabela.traducao: I'm asking you for a favor. / I'm asking you something.

erros.motivo: «Preguntar» means to ask a question; to request something, use «pedir».

erros.errado: Yo que tú, hablo con ella.
erros.certo: Yo que tú, hablaría con ella.
erros.motivo: After «yo que tú», use the conditional.

erros.errado: Debes dormir más. (trying to be gentle)
erros.motivo: The conditional softens the advice.
After «encantaría», the infinitive comes straight after, with no «de».

topicos.titulo: Degrees of courtesy when asking
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the same thing can be asked for in several ways, from the most direct to the most polite. With a friend: «Dame la llave» (direct), «¿Me das la llave?» (natural), «¿Me puedes dar la llave?». STEP 2: with someone you don't know, or in a formal setting: «¿Podría darme la llave?» or «Quisiera la llave, por favor». STEP 3: to ask for something difficult or inconvenient, use «¿Le importaría…?» (for «usted») or «¿Te importaría…?» (for «tú»): «¿Le importaría hablar más bajo?». STEP 4: «¿Sería posible…?» also works, with the infinitive: «¿Sería posible cambiar de habitación?» STEP 5: to explain a problem politely, don't point fingers: «Hay mucho ruido en la habitación» is gentler than «Usted hace mucho ruido». STEP 6: to thank someone and wrap up: «Muchas gracias por su ayuda», «Se lo agradezco mucho». STEP 7: false friend: «oficina» means office; an auto repair shop is «taller». STEP 8: «cuarto» and «habitación» both mean room; «cuarto de baño» is the bathroom. In a hotel, «habitación» is more common; at home, «cuarto» or «habitación».
topicos.comparacao: English has nothing like the «tú»/«usted» split driving this whole scale — one "you" covers a friend, a stranger, and a hotel clerk alike, so the courtesy ladder in English comes entirely from word choice ("gimme the key" → "could you give me the key" → "would you be able to give me the key, please") rather than from switching pronoun and verb forms the way «te» becomes «le» and «dame» becomes «podría darme». «Oficina» is the one vocabulary trap here: it means office, never an auto shop, which is «taller».

tabela.traducao: Give me the key.
Can you give me the key?
Could you give me the key, please?
Would you mind speaking more quietly?
Would it be possible to switch rooms?

erros.motivo: «Quiero» sounds too blunt with strangers.

erros.errado: La oficina del coche está cerrada.
erros.motivo: «Oficina» means office; an auto repair shop is «taller».
After «importaría», the infinitive comes straight after.
«Pedir» never takes «por»: you ask for something directly.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Estar + gerund, ir a + infinitive and acabar de
topicos.titulo: Estar + gerund
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to say what someone is doing right at this moment, use «estar» in the present + the gerund of the main verb: «Estoy leyendo», «Estás cocinando», «Está durmiendo». This matches English's own present continuous ("be" + "-ing") almost exactly, both in form and in meaning. STEP 2: the gerund is the verb form ending in «-ando» or «-iendo». -ar verbs: drop «-ar» and add «-ando»: «hablar → hablando», «trabajar → trabajando». STEP 3: -er and -ir verbs: drop the ending and add «-iendo»: «comer → comiendo», «escribir → escribiendo», «vivir → viviendo». STEP 4: when the stem ends in a vowel, the «i» of «-iendo» becomes «y»: «leer → leyendo», «oír → oyendo», «caer → cayendo», «construir → construyendo», «ir → yendo». STEP 5: -ir verbs that change their stem vowel in the present also change it in the gerund: «dormir → durmiendo», «pedir → pidiendo», «decir → diciendo», «venir → viniendo», «seguir → siguiendo», «sentir → sintiendo», «servir → sirviendo». Neither of these spelling quirks — the y-swap or the stem change — has anything to do with English's simple, unchanging "-ing," so they're new rules to learn, not habits you can transfer. STEP 6: the pronoun can go before «estar» or attach to the gerund, and the stress never moves: «Me estoy duchando» or «Estoy duchándome»; «Lo estoy leyendo» or «Estoy leyéndolo». STEP 7: use the gerund for actions in progress. A few state verbs don't combine well with it: «ser», «tener», «saber», «querer», «gustar». You say «Tengo hambre», never «Estoy teniendo hambre» — just like English says "I am hungry," not "I am being hungry." STEP 8: to talk about an action that's been going on for some time, use «llevar» + time + gerund: «Llevo tres meses estudiando español.» And to say something is still going on, «seguir» + gerund: «Sigo trabajando».
topicos.comparacao: This structure lines up with English present continuous almost perfectly, which makes it one of the easier patterns in the whole course. The one habit to unlearn: English often uses the continuous for a scheduled future event ("I'm traveling tomorrow," "We're having dinner at eight"), but Spanish never uses «estar + gerundio» that way — for a near-future plan, Spanish reaches for the present tense or «ir a», never the gerund. «Estoy viajando mañana» would sound wrong in a way the English sentence it's modeled on doesn't.

exemplos.ru: Ahora mismo estoy leyendo un libro.
exemplos.pt: Right now I'm reading a book.

exemplos.ru: ¿Qué estás haciendo?
exemplos.pt: What are you doing?

exemplos.ru: Mi padre está durmiendo.
exemplos.pt: My dad is sleeping.

exemplos.ru: Me estoy duchando; te llamo luego.
exemplos.pt: I'm taking a shower; I'll call you later.

erros.motivo: After «estar», the verb goes in the gerund.
«Estar a + infinitivo» doesn't exist in Spanish — don't carry it over from anywhere else.
Between vowels, the «i» becomes «y»: leyendo.
The gerund of «dormir» is «durmiendo».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Estar + gerund, ir a + infinitive and acabar de
topicos.titulo: Ir a + infinitive and acabar de + infinitive
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to talk about a plan or the near future, use «ir» in the present + «a» + infinitive: «Voy a comprar pan», «Vamos a viajar». This is Spanish's own close match to English "going to": the shape even lines up word for word, «a» doing the same job as "to." The present of «ir» is: voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van. STEP 2: the «a» is required: «Voy a comer», never «Voy comer». STEP 3: the same structure works as an invitation, like English "let's…": «Vamos a comer» means "let's eat." STEP 4: difference in use: «ir a» + infinitive is the everyday future, for plans and intentions («Esta tarde voy a estudiar»); the simple future sounds firmer or more formal and shows up a lot in predictions and promises («Mañana lloverá»). In practice, the two are often interchangeable. STEP 5: for the recent past, use «acabar de» + infinitive, with «acabar» in the present — this matches English "just" + the simple past almost one for one: «Acabo de llegar» means "I just arrived." STEP 6: the form is fixed: «acabar» in the present + «de» + infinitive. «Acaba de salir» means "he/she just left." The one trap: Spanish keeps «acabar» in the present tense even though the meaning is past — there's no Spanish equivalent of putting "acabar" itself into a past form here, the way you might expect. STEP 7: «estar a punto de» + infinitive expresses that something is about to happen: «Estoy a punto de salir» means "I'm about to leave." STEP 8: pronouns go before «ir» and «acabar», or attached to the infinitive: «Me voy a duchar / Voy a ducharme», «Lo acabo de ver / Acabo de verlo». STEP 9: «ir a» is also used for weather forecasts, in the third person: «Va a llover», «Va a nevar».
topicos.comparacao: Both of these map onto English almost one for one: «voy a comer» is "I'm going to eat," and «acabo de llegar» is "I just arrived." The one habit to watch is tense: English can say "I just arrived" with "just" riding on the simple past, but Spanish keeps «acabar» itself in the present tense no matter what — «acabé de llegar» isn't how this works, even though the meaning is clearly past.

exemplos.ru: Esta tarde voy a estudiar en la biblioteca.
exemplos.pt: This afternoon I'm going to study at the library.

exemplos.ru: Vamos a cenar en un bar cerca del cine.
exemplos.pt: We're going to have dinner at a bar near the movie theater.

exemplos.ru: Acabo de llegar a casa.
exemplos.pt: I just got home.

exemplos.ru: Va a llover; toma el paraguas.
exemplos.pt: It's going to rain; bring an umbrella.

erros.motivo: The «a» is required between «ir» and the infinitive.
With «acabar de», the verb «acabar» stays in the present.
The expression is «acabar de», with «de».
The preposition for «ir a» is always «a».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Estar + gerund, ir a + infinitive and acabar de
topicos.titulo: Choosing the structure and watching out for false friends
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to choose, think about the timing of the action: right now → «estar + gerundio»; right after → «ir a + infinitivo»; right before → «acabar de + infinitivo». STEP 2: with «todavía» (still) and «ya» (already), the gerund shows an action in progress: «Todavía estoy trabajando», «Ya estoy llegando». STEP 3: to say what isn't happening, put «no» before «estar»: «No estoy trabajando». STEP 4: in questions, the gerund comes after the verb: «¿Qué estás haciendo?», «¿Dónde estáis comiendo?» STEP 5: false friends in this lesson: «cena» isn't a movie scene; it's dinner. «Cenar» means to have dinner. A movie scene is «escena» — close enough to the English word "scene" that it's easy to mix up with «cena» in the other direction too. STEP 6: «embarazada» means pregnant, not embarrassed — this is one of the best-known traps for an English speaker, since the word looks almost exactly like "embarrassed." For embarrassed, use «avergonzada». STEP 7: «constipado» means to have a cold, not constipated in the digestive sense — another word that looks like it should mean something else. STEP 8: «pasarlo bien» means to have a good time: «¡Que lo paséis bien!» (Spain) or «¡Que lo pases bien!». STEP 9: on the phone, the most common question is «¿Qué estás haciendo?» or «¿Qué haces?», and answering with the gerund feels completely natural.
topicos.comparacao: English speakers run into «embarazada» as practically a trap built for them: it's one of the most famous false friends in Spanish precisely because it looks so close to "embarrassed" while meaning pregnant. «Cena» has the same kind of near-miss with "scene," even though the real word for a movie scene, «escena», is the one that actually resembles it.

tabela.exemplo: La cena es a las nueve.
La última escena es muy triste.

erros.motivo: «Embarazada» means pregnant.

erros.errado: Vamos a ver una cena de la película.
erros.certo: Vamos a ver una escena de la película.
erros.motivo: «Cena» means dinner; a movie scene is «escena».
For the near future, use «ir a», not the gerund of «ir».
After «estar», the verb goes in the gerund.

topicos.titulo: Mucho, poco, bastante, demasiado, todo and algún
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «mucho» and «poco» have two jobs. Before a noun, they agree in gender and number: «mucha gente», «muchos amigos», «poca agua», «pocas ideas». After a verb, they never change: «Trabajo mucho», «Duerme poco». STEP 2: «bastante» means "enough" or "quite, fairly". With a noun, it agrees only in number: «bastante dinero», «bastantes libros». With an adjective, it doesn't change and softens it: «Es bastante caro» (it's quite expensive). STEP 3: «demasiado» means excess: «demasiado calor», «demasiada gente», «demasiados coches». Before an adjective, it doesn't change and goes in front of it: «Es demasiado caro» (it's too expensive). Never say «muy demasiado». STEP 4: «suficiente» also means "enough": «Tengo suficiente tiempo», «No hay suficientes sillas». STEP 5: «todo, toda, todos, todas» need the article before the noun: «todo el día» (all day), «toda la noche» (all night), «todos los días» (every day), «todas las semanas» (every week). Without the article, these sound wrong. STEP 6: «algún» and «ningún» are shortened forms of «alguno» and «ninguno», used before a masculine singular noun: «algún día», «ningún problema». In the feminine, there's no shortening: «alguna vez», «ninguna idea». STEP 7: the double negative is normal: «No tengo nada» (I don't have anything), «No viene nadie», «No hay ningún problema». If the negative word comes before the verb, drop «no»: «Nadie viene», «Nunca estudio». STEP 8: «un poco de» + a noun you can't count: «un poco de agua», «un poco de tiempo»; «un montón de» is informal and means "loads of": «un montón de gente».
topicos.comparacao: English splits «mucho» into three words — "much" for things you can't count, "many" for things you can, "a lot" after a verb — while Spanish uses one word that simply changes its ending to agree: «mucho tiempo», «mucha agua», «muchos amigos», «Trabajo mucho». The trap is with adjectives: "very expensive" is «muy caro», never «mucho caro». And "too" is «demasiado», placed before the adjective just like in English: «demasiado caro» = "too expensive". Watch the false friend: «bastante caro» is "quite expensive", not "expensive enough".

exemplos.ru: Hay demasiada gente en el metro.
exemplos.pt: There are too many people on the subway.

exemplos.ru: Tengo suficiente tiempo para comer.
exemplos.pt: I have enough time to eat.

exemplos.ru: Estudio todos los días.
exemplos.pt: I study every day.

exemplos.ru: No tengo ningún problema.
exemplos.pt: I don't have any problem.

linhas.exemplo: Hay mucha gente en la calle.

linhas.palavra: todo el, toda la, todos los, todas las
un poco de, un montón de

erros.motivo: «Todo» agrees with «días» and needs the article: todos los días.
«Demasiado» already means "too", so it never takes «muy».
Before a masculine singular noun, «ninguno» is shortened.
«Mucho» agrees with «gente», which is feminine.

topicos.titulo: Por and para: two ways of looking
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: English often says "for" where Spanish has to choose between «por» and «para». A practical rule: «para» looks ahead, to the goal; «por» looks back, to the cause, or along the path. STEP 2: use «para» for destination: «Salgo para Madrid», «Este tren va para Sevilla». STEP 3: use «para» for purpose, what something is for: «Estudio para aprender», «Una taza para café», «¿Para qué sirve?». STEP 4: use «para» for the recipient: «Este regalo es para ti», «Trabajo para una empresa pequeña». STEP 5: use «para» for deadlines and opinions: «Tengo que terminar para el lunes» (by Monday), «Para mí, es muy fácil». STEP 6: use «por» for cause and reason: «Estoy cansado por el calor», «No salgo por la lluvia». STEP 7: use «por» for a route or a rough location (through, around, by): «Paso por tu calle», «Viajamos por España». STEP 8: use «por» for means, exchange and price: «Hablo por teléfono», «Pago diez euros por el libro», «Gracias por tu ayuda». STEP 9: use «por» for parts of the day and duration: «por la mañana» (in the morning), «por la tarde», «por la noche», «por tres días». But with an exact time, use «de»: «a las ocho de la mañana». STEP 10: learn the fixed expressions: «por favor», «por eso», «por ejemplo», «por fin», «por supuesto», «por primera vez».
topicos.comparacao: English uses "for" for almost everything that Spanish splits between «por» and «para» — that's why this pair is hard for English speakers. "A gift for you" is «para ti» (recipient), but "thanks for your help" is «por tu ayuda» (cause). "To" + verb for purpose is «para»: «Estudio para aprender», never «por aprender». And several English prepositions turn into «por»: "through/around" («por el parque»), "by" («por teléfono»), "per" («dos veces por semana»), "in the morning" («por la mañana»). Ask yourself: am I looking ahead to a goal (para) or back at a reason or along a path (por)?

exemplos.ru: Voy a la tienda para comprar pan.
exemplos.pt: I'm going to the store to buy bread.

exemplos.ru: No voy a la playa por el frío.
exemplos.pt: I'm not going to the beach because of the cold.

exemplos.ru: Este regalo es para mi madre.
exemplos.pt: This gift is for my mother.

exemplos.ru: Gracias por todo.
exemplos.pt: Thanks for everything.

linhas.exemplo: Necesito el informe para el viernes.
Para mí, es una buena idea.
Paso por tu casa a las seis.
Pago veinte euros por la camiseta.

erros.motivo: Purpose takes «para».
Thanking takes «por».
Destination takes «para»; «por» would only mean the route.
Cause takes «por».

topicos.titulo: How adverbs in -mente are formed
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: an adverb says how, when or where an action happens. Many are formed with an adjective + «-mente», the Spanish "-ly". STEP 2: take the adjective in its feminine singular form: «lento → lenta», «claro → clara», «rápido → rápida». Then add «-mente»: «lentamente», «claramente», «rápidamente». STEP 3: if the adjective doesn't change for gender (ending in -e, -l, -z, for example), just add «-mente»: «fácil → fácilmente», «feliz → felizmente», «frecuente → frecuentemente». STEP 4: the adjective's written accent stays: «rápido → rápidamente», «fácil → fácilmente». The adverb has two stressed syllables. STEP 5: when two adverbs are joined by «y», it's common (and elegant) to put «-mente» only on the last one: «lenta y claramente»; «lentamente y claramente» is also accepted. STEP 6: the adverb of «bueno» is «bien», just like "good → well". Its opposite is «mal». STEP 7: in everyday speech, many adjectives work as adverbs without changing: «Habla rápido», «Trabaja duro», «Habla claro». STEP 8: alternatives without «-mente»: «con cuidado» (carefully), «con paciencia» (patiently), «de forma tranquila» (calmly), «despacio» (slowly), «deprisa» (quickly). STEP 9: false friend: «pronto» means soon or early, not "right away" as in English. To say you're ready, use «listo» (or «preparado»). Say «Estoy listo», not «Estoy pronto».
topicos.comparacao: «-mente» is the Spanish "-ly": «claramente» = "clearly", «rápidamente» = "quickly". The difference is the starting point: English adds "-ly" to the adjective as it is, Spanish adds «-mente» to the feminine form («lento → lentamente», never «lentomente»), and the written accent stays («rápidamente», «fácilmente»). English also has an exception, "good → well", and Spanish has the same one: «bueno → bien». Watch «pronto»: in Spanish it means "soon" or "early" — "I'm ready" is «Estoy listo».

erros.motivo: «Bueno» is an adjective; the adverb is «bien».
Start from the feminine: lenta + mente.
The adjective's written accent stays in «rápidamente».
In Spanish, «pronto» means soon or early.

topicos.titulo: Que: one relative word for people and things
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: a relative word joins two sentences and avoids repeating the same noun. Two sentences: «Tengo un amigo. Mi amigo vive en Sevilla.» One sentence: «Tengo un amigo que vive en Sevilla.» STEP 2: «que» covers "who", "which" and "that": people and things, singular and plural, masculine and feminine. It never changes: «el libro que», «los libros que», «la chica que», «las chicas que». STEP 3: «que» can be the subject (who does the action: «la chica que vive aquí») or the object (what receives it: «el libro que leo»). The form is the same. STEP 4: unlike English, Spanish never leaves the relative out. "The book I'm reading" must be «el libro que leo». STEP 5: the relative comes right after the noun it describes, and that noun isn't repeated as a pronoun: «el libro que lo leo» is wrong. STEP 6: «que» without an accent is the relative; «qué» with an accent is for questions and exclamations: «¿Qué lees?» but «el libro que leo». STEP 7: with a past-tense verb, it works the same way: «La película que vimos ayer era muy larga.» (False friend: «larga» means long, not large; "large" is «grande».) STEP 8: for extra information between commas, the relative is still «que»: «Mi hermana, que vive en Lyon, viene mañana.» STEP 9: after «que», the verb stays in the indicative when the person or thing is known. The subjunctive, for things you're looking for or wishing for, comes at B1.
topicos.comparacao: English constantly leaves the relative out: "the book I'm reading", "the movie we saw". Spanish never does — «que» is required: «el libro que leo», never «el libro leo». English also chooses between "who", "which" and "that"; Spanish uses «que» for all of them, people and things alike. And once «que» is there, the noun is not repeated as a pronoun: «el libro que leo», not «el libro que lo leo».

tabela.exemplo: La chica que vive aquí es médica.
tabela.traducao: The girl who lives here is a doctor.

tabela.exemplo: El libro que leo es muy bueno.
tabela.traducao: The book I'm reading is very good.

tabela.exemplo: El compañero que trabaja conmigo es de Bilbao.
tabela.traducao: The coworker who works with me is from Bilbao.

tabela.exemplo: Las tiendas que abren tarde cierran a las diez.
tabela.traducao: The stores that open late close at ten.

tabela.exemplo: Mi hermana, que vive en Lyon, viene mañana.
tabela.traducao: My sister, who lives in Lyon, is coming tomorrow.

erros.errado: El libro que lo leo es bueno.
erros.certo: El libro que leo es bueno.
erros.motivo: «Que» already stands for the book; don't repeat it with «lo».

erros.errado: La chica que ella vive aquí es mi amiga.
erros.certo: La chica que vive aquí es mi amiga.
erros.motivo: The subject is already in «que»; «ella» is one word too many.

erros.errado: El libro qué leo es bueno.
erros.certo: El libro que leo es bueno.
erros.motivo: «Qué» with an accent is only for questions and exclamations.

erros.errado: Los vecinos que vive aquí son simpáticos.
erros.certo: Los vecinos que viven aquí son simpáticos.
erros.motivo: The verb agrees with the noun «que» stands for: «los vecinos viven».

topicos.titulo: Place and time: donde, en el que, el día en que
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: for a place, use «donde» (where): «la ciudad donde vivo». As a relative, «donde» has no accent. With an accent, «dónde» is a question: «¿Dónde vives?». STEP 2: the alternative is «en el que», «en la que», «en los que», «en las que». The article agrees with the place: «la casa en la que vivo» means the same as «la casa donde vivo». STEP 3: the preposition depends on the verb: «vivir en», «ir a», «salir de», «pasar por», «hablar de», «trabajar con». It always goes before the relative, never at the end of the sentence the way English puts it ("the house I live in"): «la casa en la que vivo». STEP 4: with «a» and «de», the article merges: «a + el = al», «de + el = del». So: «el cine al que vamos» and «el libro del que hablo». There's no merging in the feminine: «la tienda a la que voy». STEP 5: for time, use «en que» after «día», «año», «mes», «momento», «semana»: «el día en que nos conocimos», «el año en que llegué». In everyday speech you'll also hear «el día que nos conocimos». STEP 6: «la vez que» (the time that) and «cada vez que» (every time) take no preposition: «la última vez que te vi». STEP 7: «donde» can stand on its own, with no noun before it: «Vivo donde trabajo» (I live where I work). STEP 8: for movement, «adonde» also exists: «la ciudad adonde vamos». But «a la que» is the most natural choice.
topicos.comparacao: This is the big one for English speakers. English happily ends a sentence with a preposition: "the house I live in", "the movie theater we're going to", "the book I'm talking about". Spanish never does. The preposition moves to the front, before the relative: «la casa en la que vivo», «el cine al que vamos», «el libro del que hablo». «La casa que vivo en» is impossible, and «la casa que vivo» (no preposition at all) is wrong too. When in doubt about a place, «donde» works: «la casa donde vivo».

tabela.exemplo: La casa en la que vivo es pequeña.
tabela.traducao: The house I live in is small.

tabela.exemplo: El cine al que vamos está cerca.
tabela.traducao: The movie theater we're going to is nearby.

tabela.exemplo: El libro del que hablo es nuevo.
tabela.traducao: The book I'm talking about is new.

tabela.exemplo: La calle por la que paso está cerrada.
tabela.traducao: The street I walk along is closed.

tabela.exemplo: La estación de la que sale el tren es grande.
tabela.traducao: The station the train leaves from is big.

tabela.exemplo: El día en que nos conocimos llovía.
tabela.traducao: It was raining on the day we met.

erros.errado: La casa que vivo es pequeña.
erros.certo: La casa donde vivo es pequeña. / La casa en la que vivo es pequeña.
erros.motivo: The preposition «en» is missing: Spanish never drops it (or moves it to the end, as English does).

erros.errado: La ciudad dónde vivo es grande.
erros.certo: La ciudad donde vivo es grande.
erros.motivo: As a relative, «donde» has no accent.

erros.errado: El cine que fuimos ayer es nuevo.
erros.certo: El cine al que fuimos ayer es nuevo.
erros.motivo: «Ir» takes «a»; with «el» it becomes «al que».

erros.errado: El libro de el que hablo es bueno.
erros.certo: El libro del que hablo es bueno.
erros.motivo: «de + el» merges into «del».

topicos.titulo: Quien, el que, la que: people after a preposition
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: for people after a preposition, use «quien» (singular) and «quienes» (plural) — like formal English "whom": «la persona con quien hablo» (the person with whom I speak), «los chicos con quienes trabajo». STEP 2: the most common form in speech is «con el que», «con la que», «con los que», «con las que»: «la amiga con la que viajo» means the same as «la amiga con quien viajo». STEP 3: as a plain subject, with no preposition, use «que», not «quien», even though English says "who": «los chicos que llegan». «Quien» without a preposition only appears between commas, in a more formal style: «Mi hermana, quien vive en Lyon, viene mañana.» STEP 4: «el que, la que, los que, las que» with no noun before them mean "the one who, those who": «Los que llegan tarde esperan.» STEP 5: when the relative is the direct object and refers to a person, Spanish adds the personal «a»: «la chica a la que vi ayer» or «a quien vi ayer». STEP 6: the relative «cuyo» (whose) comes at B1.
topicos.comparacao: «Con quien» is formal English "with whom": "the friend with whom I travel" — which is exactly the word order Spanish requires, never "the friend I travel with". Two more differences: unlike "who", «quien» has a plural, «quienes»; and as a plain subject, Spanish uses «que», not «quien»: "the kids who arrive late" is «los chicos que llegan tarde».

erros.errado: La amiga que viajo con ella es de Cádiz.
erros.certo: La amiga con la que viajo es de Cádiz.
erros.motivo: Preposition before the relative, and no extra «ella».

erros.errado: El chico que hablo es mi primo.
erros.certo: El chico con quien hablo es mi primo.
erros.motivo: The preposition «con» is missing.

erros.errado: Los chicos quien llegan tarde esperan.
erros.certo: Los chicos que llegan tarde esperan.
erros.motivo: As a subject with no preposition, use «que».

erros.errado: Las amigas con quien viajo son brasileñas.
erros.certo: Las amigas con quienes viajo son brasileñas.
erros.motivo: The plural needs «quienes».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Health: the doctor and the pharmacy
topicos.titulo: Doler, tener dolor de and tener fiebre
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to say what hurts, use «doler» exactly like «gustar» (lesson 16). The body part is the subject and the person appears as «me, te, le»: «Me duele la cabeza.» Literally "the head hurts to me". English says "MY head hurts" — the person is the owner; Spanish makes the person the one who receives the pain. STEP 2: if the body part is plural, so is the verb: «Me duelen los pies.» STEP 3: «doler» changes the stem «o» to «ue» (duele, duelen); the infinitive is «doler». With each person: me duele, te duele, le duele, nos duele, os duele (Spain), les duele. STEP 4: with body parts, Spanish uses the article («la cabeza», «los pies»), not the possessive («mi cabeza»). English "my head", "my feet" → Spanish «la cabeza», «los pies»: the «me» already says whose it is. STEP 5: another way to say the same thing is «tener dolor de» + body part, with no article: «Tengo dolor de cabeza» (I have a headache), «Tengo dolor de estómago» (stomach ache), «Tengo dolor de espalda» (backache). «Dolor» is masculine: «un dolor fuerte». STEP 6: symptoms are said with «tener» ("to have"), with no article — unlike English "I have A fever, A cough": «Tengo fiebre», «Tengo tos», «Tengo alergia», «Tengo náuseas». STEP 7: for general states, use «estar» and «sentirse»: «Estoy mareado» (I'm dizzy), «Me siento mal», «Me encuentro mal» (I feel unwell).
